title: Kestrel reverse proxies TLS networking and load balancing
concepts: Kestrel is ASP.NET Core's cross-platform HTTP server and can run directly at the edge or behind a reverse proxy. The topology decides which component terminates TLS, validates the Host header, limits connections, and supplies the original client context.

An endpoint binds an address and port and selects permitted HTTP protocols. TLS configuration includes certificates, protocol negotiation, SNI, client-certificate requirements, and trust-chain validation; TLS pass-through and TLS termination are different network flows.

A reverse proxy commonly terminates TLS and forwards to Kestrel over a private connection. Forwarded headers can restore the external scheme, host, prefix, and client address only when received from a trusted proxy; accepting forged headers changes authentication, redirects, rate limits, and audit identity.

Kestrel limits protect resources, but defaults and behavior can differ by HTTP version, endpoint, and hosting integration. Set timeouts and size limits from workload expectations and account for limits imposed earlier by IIS, a proxy, or a load balancer.

YARP implements reverse proxying in ASP.NET Core using routes, clusters, destinations, transforms, load balancing, session affinity, and active or passive health checks. A destination being configured does not mean it is healthy or eligible for every request.

A secure deployment assigns each responsibility to a clear trust boundary: public TLS and host validation at the edge or Kestrel, narrowly trusted forwarding headers at the application, and private backend reachability. Misordered middleware or broad proxy trust can create security and redirect failures.

versionNotes.edition: ASP.NET Core 8.0.17/9.0.6 forwarded-header security change and ASP.NET Core 10 docs, checked 2026-11-14
items: Starting with ASP.NET Core 8.0.17 and 9.0.6, forwarded headers from unconfigured proxies are ignored by default. Trust proxies explicitly; clearing KnownProxies and KnownNetworks allows arbitrary peers to supply identity and scheme headers. Current Kestrel HTTP/3 support depends on platform and QUIC requirements.

scopeExclusions: IIS site, app-pool, ANCM, and Windows hosting configuration are t09-003
Azure Application Gateway, AWS ALB, nginx, and Apache syntax is vendor/server-specific and excluded from this ASP.NET Core implementation inventory
HTTP method semantics, HTTP caching, HTTP/2 framing, HTTP/3 protocol internals, and general TLS cryptography are covered by protocol and security topics
ASP.NET Core middleware APIs unrelated to proxying are in framework topics
Do not enable forwarded-header processing for untrusted direct-edge traffic; do not treat X-Forwarded headers as authenticated merely because they are present
YARP extension points beyond the named public configuration abstractions require version-specific API documentation and aren't exhaustively enumerated here
